results.name: repeat_exposure_drift
results.description: For participant-set pairs answered >=10 times (participants delimited by trial_index resetting to 0), yes rate on the 6th and later encounters of that set minus the first 5; observed > null means people become more liberal with a set the more they are queried about it (the model has no within-session dynamics), observed < null means they become stricter.
results.code:
# name: repeat_exposure_drift
# description: For participant-set pairs answered >=10 times (participants delimited by trial_index resetting to 0), yes rate on the 6th and later encounters of that set minus the first 5; observed > null means people become more liberal with a set the more they are queried about it (the model has no within-session dynamics), observed < null means they become stricter.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].astype(int).values == 0).cumsum()
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    key = pd.Series(pid.astype(str)) + "|" + pd.Series(sets)
    k = key.groupby(key).cumcount().values
    tot = key.map(key.value_counts()).values
    m = tot >= 10
    a = r[m & (k >= 5)]
    b = r[m & (k < 5)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: monotone_order_set_yes_contrast
results.description: Among sets of >=3 examples and non-example targets, yes rate for sets shown in strictly ascending or descending order minus sets shown in mixed order; observed > null means sorted presentation makes people generalise more broadly than the order-invariant model predicts from content alone, observed < null means sorted sets are read as narrower sequences.

results.name: sequence_continuation_asymmetry
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples, yes rate on the forward arithmetic continuation of the shown order (last + (last - second-last)) minus the backward continuation (first - (second - first)), targets in 1..100; observed > null (null reflects only content, model is order-invariant) means people extrapolate the shown sequence in its presented direction, observed < null means the reverse.

results.name: magnitude_outlier_neighbourhood
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples with one magnitude outlier (an end example whose gap to its neighbour is >=20 and >=2x every other gap, e.g. 100 in 31,19,49,100), yes rate on non-example targets within 5 of the outlier minus targets within 5 of the other examples; observed < null means people discount the isolated example as a stray more than the model's 10% stray rate allows, observed > null means they generalise around it more.
results.code:
# name: magnitude_outlier_neighbourhood
# description: For sets of >=3 examples with one magnitude outlier (an end example whose gap to its neighbour is >=20 and >=2x every other gap, e.g. 100 in 31,19,49,100), yes rate on non-example targets within 5 of the outlier minus targets within 5 of the other examples; observed < null means people discount the isolated example as a stray more than the model's 10% stray rate allows, observed > null means they generalise around it more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    out = {}
    for s in pd.unique(sets):
        e = sorted(int(x) for x in s.split(","))
        out[s] = (-999, -999, -999)
        if len(e) < 3:
            continue
        g = np.diff(e)
        for idx, gi, rest in ((0, g[0], g[1:]), (len(e) - 1, g[-1], g[:-1])):
            if gi >= 20 and gi >= 2 * rest.max():
                others = [x for j, x in enumerate(e) if j != idx]
                out[s] = (e[idx], min(others), max(others))
    o = pd.Series(sets).map(lambda s: out[s][0]).values
    lo = pd.Series(sets).map(lambda s: out[s][1]).values
    hi = pd.Series(sets).map(lambda s: out[s][2]).values
    valid = o > -999
    isex = np.array([str(x) in s.split(",") for x, s in zip(t, sets)])
    near_o = valid & ~isex & (np.abs(t - o) <= 5)
    near_r = valid & ~isex & ~near_o & (t >= lo - 5) & (t <= hi + 5)
    if near_o.sum() == 0 or near_r.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near_o].mean() - r[near_r].mean())

results.name: endpoint_target_salience
results.description: Over sets not containing the target, yes rate on the line endpoints (targets 1 and 100) minus yes rate on near-endpoint targets (2-5 and 96-99); observed > null means people give the endpoints a salience bonus beyond what the model's concepts assign them, observed < null means they avoid the endpoints more.
results.code:
# name: endpoint_target_salience
# description: Over sets not containing the target, yes rate on the line endpoints (targets 1 and 100) minus yes rate on near-endpoint targets (2-5 and 96-99); observed > null means people give the endpoints a salience bonus beyond what the model's concepts assign them, observed < null means they avoid the endpoints more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    isex = np.array([str(x) in s.split(",") for x, s in zip(t, sets)])
    end = ((t == 1) | (t == 100)) & ~isex
    near = (((t >= 2) & (t <= 5)) | ((t >= 96) & (t <= 99))) & ~isex
    if end.sum() == 0 or near.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[end].mean() - r[near].mean())

results.name: near_target_same_set_agreement
results.description: Among consecutive trials of the same participant with the same example set and targets within 5 of each other, the share of pairs with identical answers; observed > null means people answer neighbouring queries more consistently (a stable sampled hypothesis or response carry-over) than the model's independent trial-by-trial Bernoulli answers produce, observed < null means less consistently.
results.code:
# name: near_target_same_set_agreement
# description: Among consecutive trials of the same participant with the same example set and targets within 5 of each other, the share of pairs with identical answers; observed > null means people answer neighbouring queries more consistently (a stable sampled hypothesis or response carry-over) than the model's independent trial-by-trial Bernoulli answers produce, observed < null means less consistently.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(int).values
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(int).values
    m = (s[1:] == s[:-1]) & (ti[1:] == ti[:-1] + 1) & (np.abs(t[1:] - t[:-1]) <= 5)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.5
    return float((r[1:][m] == r[:-1][m]).mean())

results.name: mixed_parity_even_target_bias
results.description: For sets whose examples include both odd and even numbers, yes rate on even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; observed > null means people favour even numbers (or reject odd ones) more than the model's concepts imply when parity is uninformative, observed < null means they favour odd numbers more.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_even_target_bias
# description: For sets whose examples include both odd and even numbers, yes rate on even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; observed > null means people favour even numbers (or reject odd ones) more than the model's concepts imply when parity is uninformative, observed < null means they favour odd numbers more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mp = {}
    for s in pd.unique(sets):
        e = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        mp[s] = len(set(x % 2 for x in e)) == 2
    m = pd.Series(sets).map(mp).values.astype(bool)
    isex = np.array([str(x) in s.split(",") for x, s in zip(t, sets)])
    a = r[m & ~isex & (t % 2 == 0)]
    b = r[m & ~isex & (t % 2 == 1)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_target_yes
results.description: Yes rate on two-digit targets (not ending in 0, not themselves examples) whose digit reversal is one of the shown examples (e.g. 38 after 83); observed > null means people treat digit-swapped numbers as related more than the model's rule/range concepts imply, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_target_yes
# description: Yes rate on two-digit targets (not ending in 0, not themselves examples) whose digit reversal is one of the shown examples (e.g. 38 after 83); observed > null means people treat digit-swapped numbers as related more than the model's rule/range concepts imply, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",")
    tt = pd.Series(t).astype(str)
    rev = tt.str[::-1].str.lstrip("0")
    ok = (t >= 10) & (t % 10 != 0) & (t < 100)
    hit = np.array([b in e and a not in e for a, b, e in zip(tt, rev, ex)])
    m = ok & hit
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())
